highlights.titleZh: Review Finds Autonomous Agentic AI Requires Governance Shift From Content
highlights.content: In a comprehensive narrative review published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, Gregoris Mentzas of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the National Technical University of Athens evaluates the profound sociotechnical shift occurring as artificial intelligence transitions from passive generative systems to autonomous agentic systems. Drawing upon multidisciplinary literature indexed across Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar from 2020 through early 2026, alongside corporate white papers and governmental regulatory texts, the investigation synthesizes the emerging technical, application, and governance landscapes of agentic artificial intelligence. While traditional generative artificial intelligence and large language models focus primarily on statistical next-token prediction and content generation within reactive, stateless input-and-output exchanges, emerging agentic artificial intelligence systems operate within closed-loop environments characterized by adaptability, perception, planning, and goal-driven autonomy. Rather than merely producing text, software code, or imagery based on prompt-based instructions, agentic architectures utilize foundation models as reasoning engines to execute multi-step workflows, interact directly with external environments, and carry out actions without requiring continuous human prompting. The structural divergence between traditional generative models and agentic architectures is defined across four foundational technological pillars: planning and reasoning, memory and state persistence, action and tool use, and multi-agent collaboration. In agentic frameworks, reasoning mechanisms permit artificial intelligence agents to sequence operations, evaluate intermediate outcomes through self-reflection, execute logical step-by-step problem decomposition via chain of thought, and separate complex long-term objectives into structured subgoals. Concurrently, persistent memory systems provide the mechanisms required to store, retrieve, and leverage contextual history across repeated interactions, enabling continuous adaptation rather than treating each prompt as an isolated event. Through standardized application programming interfaces and executable environments, agents actively deploy external digital tools to inspect environments and enact concrete state changes across external software stacks. Furthermore, multi-agent frameworks facilitate structured collaboration, dynamic task delegation, and functional specialization among multiple discrete agents, allowing distributed digital teams to simulate complex institutional environments and coordinate long-horizon workflows across diverse operational domains. The emergence of agentic infrastructure has catalyzed new interoperability initiatives, notably the Model Context Protocol introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 and the Agent-to-Agent protocol released by Google in April 2025. The Model Context Protocol provides an open specification designed to connect autonomous agents with external digital tools and specialized execution interfaces, whereas the Agent-to-Agent protocol establishes structured agent cards that document agent identities, operational skills, and functional capabilities for automated system discovery. However, the review emphasizes that neither protocol has been formally submitted to recognized international standards bodies such as IEEE, ISO/IEC JTC 1, or the World Wide Web Consortium. Despite rapid integration across major developer frameworks including LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen, and Vertex AI Agent Builder, substantial interoperability barriers persist across both specifications. Most notably, the lack of a shared identity or unified credential layer prevents agents discovered through the Agent-to-Agent protocol from seamlessly authenticating when calling tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol, while existing threat models remain immature compared to established web security standards. ...

highlights.content: ![AI Orchestration Is Only Half the Equation](https://itbrief.co.uk/uploads/story/2026/11/26/unnamed-story-cea1754da0fb69bd.webp) [KEVIN BOHAN Director of Product Marketing Denodo](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kevin-bohan) ![Kevin Bohan](https://itbrief.co.uk/uploads/story/2026/11/26/unnamed-story-cea1754da0fb69bd.webp) As companies move from standalone AI assistants to systems of agents, orchestration is becoming a more important architectural decision. A recent Gartner report, Selecting AI Agent Orchestration Technologies for Multiagent Systems, [available to Gartner clients](https://www.gartner.com/document-reader/document/8072165?ref=pubsite), by Keith Guttridge and Shiva Varma, helps explain why that decision is getting harder. Gartner identifies three broad styles of multiagent systems and seven different meanings of AI agent orchestration. The report also argues that most enterprises are unlikely to meet all of their agentic AI needs with a single technology stack. That has a clear implication. Organisations need to choose orchestration technologies that fit the agent patterns they plan to use, the controls they require, and the way they intend to operate. But orchestration is only part of the architecture. Capabilities such as model routing, workflow sequencing, tool calling, agent delegation, and agent-to-agent coordination are likely to become more widely available across platforms. Products will still differ in reliability, ease of use, scalability, observability, and cost. Those differences will matter, particularly in high-risk or regulated environments. Over time, however, a more durable source of advantage may be the organization's ability to deliver live, trusted, and governed business context from across distributed systems at the moment an agent needs it. **The integration problem hiding inside agent adoption** Most organizations are still experimenting with agentic AI. Teams are connecting agents to applications, APIs, data platforms, MCP servers, retrieval pipelines, and custom tools. At first, this often looks like progress. One team connects an agent to a CRM. Another builds access to an ERP system. A third creates retrieval logic for a warehouse or lakehouse. Each use case may appear manageable on its own. The problem emerges when those projects begin to multiply. Every agent or orchestration platform can end up with its own data connections, semantic mappings, transformations, access rules, quality checks, and audit logic. The organization begins to recreate point-to-point integration, this time across an expanding estate of agents. That risk deserves more attention than it receives. A connection built for one agent may be quick to create. Ten similar connections across different teams are harder to manage. A hundred can become a lasting source of technical debt, especially when the logic is embedded across prompts, workflows, MCP servers, custom tools, and platform-specific configurations. The architectural goal should not be limited to making the first agent work. It should also prevent the hundredth agent from requiring the hundredth set of integrations, definitions, and controls. **A clearer division of responsibility** A scalable approach requires a separation between the work agents perform and the enterprise context they depend on. Agents and orchestration platforms should focus on reasoning, planning, task coordination, workflow execution, and the selection of models and tools. That is where business logic and agent behavior belong. They should not also become the enterprise data integration and governance layer. A separate context foundation should manage how information is found, interpreted, secured, and delivered. It should provide consistent business meaning, reusable integration logic, runtime authorization, provenance, lineage, and access to current operational and analytical information. highlights.titleZh: Krafton Releases In-House AI Model Raon-1 Mini < IT·Gaming < 기사본문 - The Elec Inc.
highlights.content: ![A performance comparison chart released by Krafton. (Source: Krafton)](https://cdn.thelec.net/news/photo/202611/15933_16308_5530.png) Krafton released the full version of its internally developed large language model (LLM), Raon-1 mini, on Nov. 25. According to the company, Raon-1 mini is an artificial intelligence (AI) model developed entirely in-house, from model architecture design to training. It adopts a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture that activates only 4 billion of its 30 billion parameters for computation. Combined with Krafton’s proprietary linear attention technology, the architecture improves response speed and reduces inference costs. Krafton said the full version offers improved reasoning and complex task execution capabilities compared with the preview version. It scored 64.9 on MultiChallenge, a benchmark measuring a model’s ability to follow user instructions and constraints across multiple conversational turns, up 5.9 points from the preview version. According to Krafton, the model outperformed all six comparable overseas models. The model also scored 72.3 and 55.9 on GDPval and BrowseComp Plus, respectively, which evaluate AI agents’ task execution capabilities. It achieved the highest scores among comparable MoE models in both benchmarks. Krafton also added adjustable reasoning capabilities. Users can select from six reasoning levels depending on task complexity. The model answers simple questions without a reasoning process while allocating more computational resources to complex tasks. Krafton released Raon-1 mini on AI model-sharing platform Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Anyone can download the model for free and use it for research and commercial service development. The company also provides an environment for testing the model and an application programming interface (API). Since launching its AI model brand Raon in April, Krafton has released open-source AI models for speech and vision applications. The company plans to introduce Raon-1, a larger model than Raon-1 mini, and a real-time bidirectional speech model capable of listening and responding to users simultaneously. ![kimsungjin의 프로필 이미지](https://cdn.thelec.net/image/newsroom/default-user.png) [View other news](https://www.thelec.net/news/articleList.html?sc_area=I&sc_word=harang&view_type=sm)

highlights.content: A comprehensive review of the artificial intelligence literature indicates that agentic artificial intelligence represents a structural transition beyond passive generative models and classical rule-based systems by coupling multi-step reasoning, hierarchical memory, dynamic tool use, and multi-agent coordination. Published in the journal Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering by Pejman Peykani, Sanly Ghanidel, Iman Javadi-Sisi, Vaclav Snasel, and Seyedali Mirjalili, the study synthesizes the architectural, infrastructural, and evaluative dimensions required to support autonomous systems capable of acting across complex, open-ended environments. The researchers examine how modern agentic systems overcome the core historical limitations of early symbolic software and pure text generators by integrating goal-directed execution loops with external computational resources. Historically, classical artificial intelligence agents developed during the 1980s functioned on strict logical rules and symbolic architectures, such as the Belief-Desire-Intention framework where intentions served to maintain commitments to long-term plans. Although these early systems provided transparent reasoning in structured environments like production planning and social simulations, their rigid state-based memory prevented dynamic adaptation to continuous empirical data. The subsequent emergence of deep learning and large language models demonstrated remarkable capabilities in fluent text synthesis, basic programming, and in-context learning. However, these autoregressive models remained fundamentally reactive, lacking persistent goal-setting, temporal memory, and mechanisms to interact directly with external environments. Early hybrid attempts, categorized as generative agents, introduced basic task chaining and tool execution, but single-agent architectures frequently encountered performance bottlenecks when handling intricate, long-horizon workflows. To overcome these functional constraints, agentic artificial intelligence relies on four interdependent pillars: multi-step reasoning, persistent memory, purposeful tool utilization, and active interaction. For complex problem solving, structured reasoning frameworks such as Chain of Thought and Tree of Thought enable agents to decompose complicated objectives into manageable subproblems, evaluate parallel branches, and backtrack when intermediate steps fail. Simultaneously, memory architectures extend beyond the static parametric weights of neural models and transient context windows by incorporating external retrieval-based vector stores and structured databases. In multi-agent configurations, systems assign distinct roles—such as project managers, domain specialists, and evaluators—to distribute computational workloads, coordinate actions through shared memory, and regulate execution across extended tasks. The review delineates a unified six-stage architectural framework that governs the lifecycle of an agentic system, progressing through perception, role definition, memory hierarchy, planning, action, and online self-improvement. Perception serves as the foundational interface, where language and multimodal models interpret textual, visual, and auditory inputs to formulate internal representations and predict future environmental states. Clear role specification establishes behavioral constraints, operational objectives, and domain boundaries for individual agents, facilitating targeted alignment and auditing through structured coordination frameworks. highlights.titleZh: OpenAI's GPT-Live-1.1 tops Voice Arena's Jarvis Bench, but humans still win the call
highlights.content: ![OpenAI’s GPT-Live-1.1 tops Voice Arena’s Jarvis Bench, but humans still win the call](https://static.cryptobriefing.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/26164307/library-openai-s-gpt-live-1-1-tops-voice-arena-s-jarvis-bench-bu.jpg) # OpenAI’s GPT-Live-1.1 tops Voice Arena’s Jarvis Bench, but humans still win the call FoxTPNL / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0) OpenAI's newest voice model took first place on a live-call benchmark, though raters still preferred human agents and scored Gemini higher on call handling [OpenAI](https://cryptobriefing.com/markets/openai/)’s GPT-Live-1.1 has taken first place on Voice Arena’s Jarvis Bench, a benchmark built around live phone calls rather than tidy lab prompts. There is a catch. The human raters scoring those calls still preferred actual human agents, and they rated Gemini’s call handling higher than OpenAI’s. ## What GPT-Live-1.1 actually does GPT-Live-1.1 arrived in OpenAI’s API on or around November 19, 2026. It is the successor to GPT-Live-1. The model is full-duplex, meaning it can listen and talk at the same moment. Older voice systems tend to work in turn: you speak, you stop, the machine answers. A full-duplex model can handle interruptions and overlapping speech, which is how people actually talk to each other. OpenAI has also pointed to better transcription accuracy and more consistent accents across multiple languages. The accent fix targets a familiar quirk of voice AI, where a model’s accent can drift mid-conversation. The API launch was not the model’s debut. GPT-Live-1.1 had already become the default voice model for ChatGPT Plus and Pro subscribers starting October 15, 2026. ### AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing. Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy. ## The pricing move developers will notice Active use of GPT-Live-1.1 costs $0.05 per minute. The more interesting number is the new standby mode, priced at $0.02 per minute. Standby kicks in after a configurable idle timeout. Developers can decide how long a quiet line sits at full price before the cheaper rate applies. ## How Jarvis Bench keeps score Voice Arena’s Jarvis Bench tests voice agents under practical, real-world conditions. It runs live calls and measures how often agents succeed at tasks such as booking airline travel. The benchmark also relies on human judgment. Raters cast Elo-style votes, the same basic system used to rank chess players, where head-to-head matchups determine relative standing. Jarvis Bench also puts AI agents side by side with human-driven interactions. GPT-Live-1.1 beat its machine competitors on the benchmark. When the comparison included real people, raters still sided with the humans. Gemini, [Google](https://cryptobriefing.com/markets/alphabet/)’s model family, also earned higher marks than GPT-Live-1.1 on call handling in certain metrics. As of November 26, 2026, OpenAI had not published detailed Jarvis Bench leaderboard scores or publicly confirmed the model’s results there. **Disclosure:** This article was edited by Diego Almada Lopez. highlights.titleZh: Model-Managed Context: GPT-6.1 Sol 21% to 56% (NVIDIA) | explainx.ai Blog
highlights.content: NVIDIA researchers gave four frontier models control over their own context window, and one of them nearly tripled its score. At a 32K-token budget on OfficeQA Pro v2, GPT-6.1 Sol rose from 21% to 56% when it decided for itself when to compact its history, according to the paper ["Letting Models Manage Their Own Context: Where We Stand"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34147?ref=explainx) (arXiv 2611.34147, November 25, 2026). The result is real but narrow. It holds for one model, one benchmark and a tight budget, and it fades as the window grows. This post covers what the paper did, what each model did differently, what the numbers do and do not show, and what a team building agents can test this week. ## TL;DR: what NVIDIA found | Question | Answer from the paper | |---|---| | What was tested? | Model-driven vs harness-driven context compaction in NVIDIA's open-source NOOA harness | | Which models? | GPT-6.1 Sol, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Claude Opus 5.5 | | Headline result | GPT-6.1 Sol: 21% to 56% on OfficeQA Pro v2 at a 32K budget | | Token savings | Kimi K3: up to 41% fewer input tokens; 36M vs 62M cumulative at 32K | | Who ignored the tool? | Opus 5.5 edited its context in only 4% of tasks | | Inference finding | Suffix KV-cache reuse cut prefill compute 4 to 15% per request, with no measured accuracy change | | Biggest caveat | Small benchmarks: 90 questions and 22 competitions | ## What does "model-managed context" mean? ![A broad fan of paper strips folding into a compact accordion, picturing how model-managed context compacts agent history](https://explainx.ai/images/blog-library/context-compression.webp)A broad fan of paper strips folding into a compact accordion, picturing how model-managed context compacts agent history Most agent harnesses manage context on the model's behalf. When the window fills up, the harness triggers a compaction step. The model only writes the summary. Everything else is decided by code. The NVIDIA team studied the alternative. The model gets a context API and decides when to compact and what to compress. The paper describes the setup in the NOOA harness, short for NVIDIA Labs Object-Oriented Agents, an open-source research preview where an agent is a single Python class. NVIDIA's own [developer blog on harness design](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/six-agent-harness-capabilities-for-higher-model-performance/?ref=explainx) lists "model-callable harness APIs" as one of six capabilities of the harness, and this paper tests that idea at scale. The two strategies differ in concrete ways. - **Harness-driven baseline.** At 80% of the context budget, the harness summarizes earlier history. It keeps the initial instructions and the 10 most recent events. - **Model-driven.** The model sees a live context-usage indicator, an instruction to consider compacting at 85% usage, and a context-pressure warning as the limit nears. Its main tool is a `collapse` call that replaces a range of events with a summary. - **Archive, not delete.** Collapsed events are archived. The model can retrieve any of them later by its original tag. - **Hard budgets.** Each budget, from 8K to 512K tokens, is a hard request-size limit. If a request exceeds it, a fallback drops the oldest events and retries. After three failures the run counts as wrong. If you want the background on why this matters, our post on [Apple's SelfCompact](https://explainx.ai/blog/apple-selfcompact-self-compacting-language-model-agents-context-2026) covered the same question from a different angle: should the agent decide when to compress itself. NVIDIA's earlier study, covered in [NVIDIA Says You Don't Need Long Context](https://explainx.ai/blog/nvidia-you-dont-need-long-context-compaction-sssm-arxiv-november-2026), argued that frequent compaction can match full-history accuracy at lower cost. ## The benchmarks: OfficeQA Pro v2 and MLE-bench Lite The paper uses two task families. **OfficeQA Pro v2** has 90 questions about U.S. federal receipts and exp...

The company has secured approximately 700 gross megawatts of data center capacity for delivery by the end of 2027. NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platform remains central to AI training, inference and agentic workloads as customers scale model deployment. In the third quarter of fiscal 2027, revenues rose 103% year over year to $115.84 billion, with Rubin joining Blackwell Ultra as a source of growth. highlights.content: # LLM Meaning: Definition, Examples, Uses & How It Works ![LLM Meaning: Definition, Examples, Uses & How It Works](https://wordconfusion.com/wp-content/smush-webp/2026/11/llm-meaning-1024x572.png.webp) A student sees “LLM” in a tech headline and then spots “LL.M.” on a lawyer’s business card. Both abbreviations look almost identical, yet they point to two separate worlds. One describes software that writes text, while the other describes an advanced law degree. The **llm meaning** most people search for today is “large language model,” the technology behind modern AI chatbots. This guide explains the definition, how these models work, common examples, everyday uses, and the main limits. Writers using AI tools can also read our [humanize ai text for blogs](https://wordconfusion.com/humanize-ai-text-for-blogs/) guide. By the end, you will know which meaning fits any sentence and how to use the term correctly. ## Quick Answer: What Does LLM Mean? **LLM means “large language model,” a type of AI trained on huge amounts of text to predict words.** It reads a prompt and produces new text, answers, summaries, or code in response. In legal and academic settings, LL.M. instead means Master of Laws, a postgraduate law degree. Context almost always tells readers which of these meanings a writer intends. ## LLM Meaning at a Glance LLM has two main meanings in modern English, plus a few rare uses in niche fields. The table below shows the most common meanings and where each one usually appears: | Abbreviation | Full Form | Field | Example Context | |---|---|---|---| | LLM | Large language model | Artificial intelligence | Tech news, AI tools | | LL.M. | Master of Laws | Law and education | Lawyer profiles, universities | | LLM | Lifelong learning model | Education research | Academic papers | The first meaning dominates online searches, while the law degree appears mostly in legal and university writing. ### LLM in Artificial Intelligence In AI, a large language model is software trained on billions of words from books and websites. It learns patterns in language, such as which words usually follow others in a sentence. The model then uses those patterns to write replies that read like human text. ### LL.M. in Law LL.M. comes from the Latin phrase “Legum Magister,” which translates to Master of Laws in English. Lawyers usually earn it after a first law degree to specialize in tax, international, or business law. The doubled “L” in the abbreviation reflects the Latin plural “legum,” meaning “of laws.” ## What Is a Large Language Model? A large language model is a statistical system that predicts the next piece of text. The word “large” refers to the huge training data and the billions of internal settings, called parameters. The word “language” shows that the model works with words, sentences, and other written symbols. > In simple words, an LLM is a giant autocomplete system that learned language from reading text. ### Key Characteristics of an LLM Several traits separate a large language model from older and smaller language software: - An LLM trains on massive text collections that often include books, websites, articles, and computer code. - Each model holds billions of parameters, which store the patterns it learned during its long training process. - Most modern LLMs use a transformer design, which helps them track relationships between distant words in text. - An LLM produces fresh text for each prompt instead of copying stored answers from a fixed database. - Many LLMs handle several tasks, including writing, translating, summarizing, coding, and answering open questions. These traits explain why LLMs can write essays, emails, and code with one single underlying system. ### Where the Term Came From Researchers used the phrase “language model” for decades before the word “large” joined the label. The 2017 research paper “Attention Is All You Need” introduced the transformer design that most current models use. As models grew to billi...

No use, distribution or reproduction is permitted which does not comply with these terms. # Trustworthy agentic AI systems: navigating the risks and # governance of autonomous AI #### Gregoris Mentzas* School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Institute of Communication and Computer Systems (ICCS), National Technical University of Athens, Athens, Greece Artificial Intelligence is evolving from the passive content generation of Generative AI (GenAI) to Agentic AI (AgAI) systems which are increasingly characterized by autonomy, adaptability, and goal-driven reasoning. AI Agents.content: In a comprehensive narrative review published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, Gregoris Mentzas of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the National Technical University of Athens evaluates the profound sociotechnical shift occurring as artificial intelligence transitions from passive generative systems to autonomous agentic systems. Drawing upon multidisciplinary literature indexed across Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar from 2020 through early 2026, alongside corporate white papers and governmental regulatory texts, the investigation synthesizes the emerging technical, application, and governance landscapes of agentic artificial intelligence. While traditional generative artificial intelligence and large language models focus primarily on statistical next-token prediction and content generation within reactive, stateless input-and-output exchanges, emerging agentic artificial intelligence systems operate within closed-loop environments characterized by adaptability, perception, planning, and goal-driven autonomy. Rather than merely producing text, software code, or imagery based on prompt-based instructions, agentic architectures utilize foundation models as reasoning engines to execute multi-step workflows, interact directly with external environments, and carry out actions without requiring continuous human prompting. The structural divergence between traditional generative models and agentic architectures is defined across four foundational technological pillars: planning and reasoning, memory and state persistence, action and tool use, and multi-agent collaboration. In agentic frameworks, reasoning mechanisms permit artificial intelligence agents to sequence operations, evaluate intermediate outcomes through self-reflection, execute logical step-by-step problem decomposition via chain of thought, and separate complex long-term objectives into structured subgoals. Concurrently, persistent memory systems provide the mechanisms required to store, retrieve, and leverage contextual history across repeated interactions, enabling continuous adaptation rather than treating each prompt as an isolated event. Through standardized application programming interfaces and executable environments, agents actively deploy external digital tools to inspect environments and enact concrete state changes across external software stacks. Furthermore, multi-agent frameworks facilitate structured collaboration, dynamic task delegation, and functional specialization among multiple discrete agents, allowing distributed digital teams to simulate complex institutional environments and coordinate long-horizon workflows across diverse operational domains. The emergence of agentic infrastructure has catalyzed new interoperability initiatives, notably the Model Context Protocol introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 and the Agent-to-Agent protocol released by Google in April 2025. The Model Context Protocol provides an open specification designed to connect autonomous agents with external digital tools and specialized execution interfaces, whereas the Agent-to-Agent protocol establishes structured agent cards that document agent identities, operational skills, and functional capabilities for automated system discovery. However, the review emphasizes that neither protocol has been formally submitted to recognized international standards bodies such as IEEE, ISO/IEC JTC 1, or the World Wide Web Consortium. Despite rapid integration across major developer frameworks including LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen, and Vertex AI Agent Builder, substantial interoperability barriers persist across both specifications. AI Agents.content: ![AI Orchestration Is Only Half the Equation](https://itbrief.co.uk/uploads/story/2026/11/26/unnamed-story-cea1754da0fb69bd.webp) [KEVIN BOHAN Director of Product Marketing Denodo](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kevin-bohan) ![Kevin Bohan](https://itbrief.co.uk/uploads/story/2026/11/26/unnamed-story-cea1754da0fb69bd.webp) As companies move from standalone AI assistants to systems of agents, orchestration is becoming a more important architectural decision. A recent Gartner report, Selecting AI Agent Orchestration Technologies for Multiagent Systems, [available to Gartner clients](https://www.gartner.com/document-reader/document/8072165?ref=pubsite), by Keith Guttridge and Shiva Varma, helps explain why that decision is getting harder. Gartner identifies three broad styles of multiagent systems and seven different meanings of AI agent orchestration. The report also argues that most enterprises are unlikely to meet all of their agentic AI needs with a single technology stack. That has a clear implication. Organisations need to choose orchestration technologies that fit the agent patterns they plan to use, the controls they require, and the way they intend to operate. But orchestration is only part of the architecture. Capabilities such as model routing, workflow sequencing, tool calling, agent delegation, and agent-to-agent coordination are likely to become more widely available across platforms. Products will still differ in reliability, ease of use, scalability, observability, and cost. Those differences will matter, particularly in high-risk or regulated environments. Over time, however, a more durable source of advantage may be the organization's ability to deliver live, trusted, and governed business context from across distributed systems at the moment an agent needs it. **The integration problem hiding inside agent adoption** Most organizations are still experimenting with agentic AI. Teams are connecting agents to applications, APIs, data platforms, MCP servers, retrieval pipelines, and custom tools. At first, this often looks like progress. One team connects an agent to a CRM. Another builds access to an ERP system. A third creates retrieval logic for a warehouse or lakehouse. Each use case may appear manageable on its own. The problem emerges when those projects begin to multiply. Every agent or orchestration platform can end up with its own data connections, semantic mappings, transformations, access rules, quality checks, and audit logic. The organization begins to recreate point-to-point integration, this time across an expanding estate of agents. That risk deserves more attention than it receives. A connection built for one agent may be quick to create. Ten similar connections across different teams are harder to manage. A hundred can become a lasting source of technical debt, especially when the logic is embedded across prompts, workflows, MCP servers, custom tools, and platform-specific configurations. The architectural goal should not be limited to making the first agent work. It should also prevent the hundredth agent from requiring the hundredth set of integrations, definitions, and controls. **A clearer division of responsibility** A scalable approach requires a separation between the work agents perform and the enterprise context they depend on. That is where business logic and agent behavior belong. They should not also become the enterprise data integration and governance layer. A separate context foundation should manage how information is found, interpreted, secured, and delivered. It should provide consistent business meaning, reusable integration logic, runtime authorization, provenance, lineage, and access to current operational and analytical information. AI Agents.content: A comprehensive review of the artificial intelligence literature indicates that agentic artificial intelligence represents a structural transition beyond passive generative models and classical rule-based systems by coupling multi-step reasoning, hierarchical memory, dynamic tool use, and multi-agent coordination. Published in the journal Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering by Pejman Peykani, Sanly Ghanidel, Iman Javadi-Sisi, Vaclav Snasel, and Seyedali Mirjalili, the study synthesizes the architectural, infrastructural, and evaluative dimensions required to support autonomous systems capable of acting across complex, open-ended environments. The researchers examine how modern agentic systems overcome the core historical limitations of early symbolic software and pure text generators by integrating goal-directed execution loops with external computational resources. Historically, classical artificial intelligence agents developed during the 1980s functioned on strict logical rules and symbolic architectures, such as the Belief-Desire-Intention framework where intentions served to maintain commitments to long-term plans. Although these early systems provided transparent reasoning in structured environments like production planning and social simulations, their rigid state-based memory prevented dynamic adaptation to continuous empirical data. The subsequent emergence of deep learning and large language models demonstrated remarkable capabilities in fluent text synthesis, basic programming, and in-context learning. However, these autoregressive models remained fundamentally reactive, lacking persistent goal-setting, temporal memory, and mechanisms to interact directly with external environments. Early hybrid attempts, categorized as generative agents, introduced basic task chaining and tool execution, but single-agent architectures frequently encountered performance bottlenecks when handling intricate, long-horizon workflows. To overcome these functional constraints, agentic artificial intelligence relies on four interdependent pillars: multi-step reasoning, persistent memory, purposeful tool utilization, and active interaction. For complex problem solving, structured reasoning frameworks such as Chain of Thought and Tree of Thought enable agents to decompose complicated objectives into manageable subproblems, evaluate parallel branches, and backtrack when intermediate steps fail. Simultaneously, memory architectures extend beyond the static parametric weights of neural models and transient context windows by incorporating external retrieval-based vector stores and structured databases. In multi-agent configurations, systems assign distinct roles—such as project managers, domain specialists, and evaluators—to distribute computational workloads, coordinate actions through shared memory, and regulate execution across extended tasks. The review delineates a unified six-stage architectural framework that governs the lifecycle of an agentic system, progressing through perception, role definition, memory hierarchy, planning, action, and online self-improvement. Perception serves as the foundational interface, where language and multimodal models interpret textual, visual, and auditory inputs to formulate internal representations and predict future environmental states. Clear role specification establishes behavioral constraints, operational objectives, and domain boundaries for individual agents, facilitating targeted alignment and auditing through structured coordination frameworks. Memory operations actively balance short-term context with long-term external stores, while planning mechanisms translate overarching targets into ordered action sequences. These plans culminate in concrete environmental actions, such as calling application programming interfaces, executing shell commands, or navigating software graphical user interfaces, before returning feedback signals into continuous learning modules. (Source: Krafton)](https://cdn.thelec.net/news/photo/202611/15933_16308_5530.png) Krafton released the full version of its internally developed large language model (LLM), Raon-1 mini, on Nov. 25. According to the company, Raon-1 mini is an artificial intelligence (AI) model developed entirely in-house, from model architecture design to training. It adopts a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture that activates only 4 billion of its 30 billion parameters for computation. Combined with Krafton’s proprietary linear attention technology, the architecture improves response speed and reduces inference costs. Krafton said the full version offers improved reasoning and complex task execution capabilities compared with the preview version. It scored 64.9 on MultiChallenge, a benchmark measuring a model’s ability to follow user instructions and constraints across multiple conversational turns, up 5.9 points from the preview version. According to Krafton, the model outperformed all six comparable overseas models. The model also scored 72.3 and 55.9 on GDPval and BrowseComp Plus, respectively, which evaluate AI agents’ task execution capabilities. It achieved the highest scores among comparable MoE models in both benchmarks. Krafton also added adjustable reasoning capabilities. Users can select from six reasoning levels depending on task complexity. The model answers simple questions without a reasoning process while allocating more computational resources to complex tasks. Krafton released Raon-1 mini on AI model-sharing platform Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Anyone can download the model for free and use it for research and commercial service development. The company also provides an environment for testing the model and an application programming interface (API). Since launching its AI model brand Raon in April, Krafton has released open-source AI models for speech and vision applications. The company plans to introduce Raon-1, a larger model than Raon-1 mini, and a real-time bidirectional speech model capable of listening and responding to users simultaneously. ![kimsungjin의 프로필 이미지](https://cdn.thelec.net/image/newsroom/default-user.png) [View other news](https://www.thelec.net/news/articleList.html?sc_area=I&sc_word=harang&view_type=sm)

There is a catch. The human raters scoring those calls still preferred actual human agents, and they rated Gemini’s call handling higher than OpenAI’s. ## What GPT-Live-1.1 actually does GPT-Live-1.1 arrived in OpenAI’s API on or around November 19, 2026. It is the successor to GPT-Live-1. The model is full-duplex, meaning it can listen and talk at the same moment. Older voice systems tend to work in turn: you speak, you stop, the machine answers. A full-duplex model can handle interruptions and overlapping speech, which is how people actually talk to each other. OpenAI has also pointed to better transcription accuracy and more consistent accents across multiple languages. The accent fix targets a familiar quirk of voice AI, where a model’s accent can drift mid-conversation. The API launch was not the model’s debut. GPT-Live-1.1 had already become the default voice model for ChatGPT Plus and Pro subscribers starting October 15, 2026. ### AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing. Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy. ## The pricing move developers will notice Active use of GPT-Live-1.1 costs $0.05 per minute. The more interesting number is the new standby mode, priced at $0.02 per minute. Standby kicks in after a configurable idle timeout. Developers can decide how long a quiet line sits at full price before the cheaper rate applies. ## How Jarvis Bench keeps score Voice Arena’s Jarvis Bench tests voice agents under practical, real-world conditions. It runs live calls and measures how often agents succeed at tasks such as booking airline travel. The benchmark also relies on human judgment. Raters cast Elo-style votes, the same basic system used to rank chess players, where head-to-head matchups determine relative standing. LLMs.content: NVIDIA researchers gave four frontier models control over their own context window, and one of them nearly tripled its score. When the window fills up, the harness triggers a compaction step. The model only writes the summary. Everything else is decided by code. The NVIDIA team studied the alternative. The model gets a context API and decides when to compact and what to compress. The paper describes the setup in the NOOA harness, short for NVIDIA Labs Object-Oriented Agents, an open-source research preview where an agent is a single Python class. NVIDIA's own [developer blog on harness design](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/six-agent-harness-capabilities-for-higher-model-performance/?ref=explainx) lists "model-callable harness APIs" as one of six capabilities of the harness, and this paper tests that idea at scale. The model can retrieve any of them later by its original tag. - **Hard budgets.** Each budget, from 8K to 512K tokens, is a hard request-size limit. If a request exceeds it, a fallback drops the oldest events and retries. After three failures the run counts as wrong. LLMs.content: # LLM Meaning: Definition, Examples, Uses & How It Works ![LLM Meaning: Definition, Examples, Uses & How It Works](https://wordconfusion.com/wp-content/smush-webp/2026/11/llm-meaning-1024x572.png.webp) A student sees “LLM” in a tech headline and then spots “LL.M.” on a lawyer’s business card. Both abbreviations look almost identical, yet they point to two separate worlds. One describes software that writes text, while the other describes an advanced law degree. The **llm meaning** most people search for today is “large language model,” the technology behind modern AI chatbots. This guide explains the definition, how these models work, common examples, everyday uses, and the main limits. Writers using AI tools can also read our [humanize ai text for blogs](https://wordconfusion.com/humanize-ai-text-for-blogs/) guide. By the end, you will know which meaning fits any sentence and how to use the term correctly. ## Quick Answer: What Does LLM Mean? **LLM means “large language model,” a type of AI trained on huge amounts of text to predict words.** It reads a prompt and produces new text, answers, summaries, or code in response. In legal and academic settings, LL.M. instead means Master of Laws, a postgraduate law degree. Context almost always tells readers which of these meanings a writer intends. ## LLM Meaning at a Glance LLM has two main meanings in modern English, plus a few rare uses in niche fields. The table below shows the most common meanings and where each one usually appears: | Abbreviation | Full Form | Field | Example Context | |---|---|---|---| | LLM | Large language model | Artificial intelligence | Tech news, AI tools | | LL.M. | Master of Laws | Law and education | Lawyer profiles, universities | | LLM | Lifelong learning model | Education research | Academic papers | The first meaning dominates online searches, while the law degree appears mostly in legal and university writing. ### LLM in Artificial Intelligence In AI, a large language model is software trained on billions of words from books and websites. It learns patterns in language, such as which words usually follow others in a sentence. The model then uses those patterns to write replies that read like human text. ### LL.M. in Law LL.M. comes from the Latin phrase “Legum Magister,” which translates to Master of Laws in English. Lawyers usually earn it after a first law degree to specialize in tax, international, or business law. The doubled “L” in the abbreviation reflects the Latin plural “legum,” meaning “of laws.” ## What Is a Large Language Model? A large language model is a statistical system that predicts the next piece of text. The word “large” refers to the huge training data and the billions of internal settings, called parameters. The word “language” shows that the model works with words, sentences, and other written symbols. > In simple words, an LLM is a giant autocomplete system that learned language from reading text. ### Key Characteristics of an LLM Several traits separate a large language model from older and smaller language software: - An LLM trains on massive text collections that often include books, websites, articles, and computer code. - Each model holds billions of parameters, which store the patterns it learned during its long training process. - Most modern LLMs use a transformer design, which helps them track relationships between distant words in text. - An LLM produces fresh text for each prompt instead of copying stored answers from a fixed database. - Many LLMs handle several tasks, including writing, translating, summarizing, coding, and answering open questions. These traits explain why LLMs can write essays, emails, and code with one single underlying system. ### Where the Term Came From Researchers used the phrase “language model” for decades before the word “large” joined the label. LLMs.title: Toolkit Uses Large Language Models to Generate Differentially Private
LLMs.titleZh: Toolkit Uses Large Language Models to Generate Differentially Private
LLMs.content: Researchers have developed LEGEND, an open-source software toolkit that uses a large language model to construct synthetic graphs under central edge differential privacy while preserving fine-grained connectivity patterns. Differential privacy provides rigorous mathematical bounds on the disclosure risk of individual records within shared datasets, but adapting these privacy guarantees to graph structures has historically constrained data utility. Traditional graph synthesis algorithms rely on fixed stochastic frameworks, such as stochastic Kronecker graphs, hierarchical random graphs, or block two-level Erdős-Rényi models, which often fail to capture complex empirical topologies beyond their rigid mathematical assumptions. By inserting a pretrained language model strictly into the construction step after degree sanitisation, LEGEND achieves substantial improvements in edge-count precision and degree-distribution fidelity across benchmark subgraphs of twenty to sixty nodes. Because the model operates entirely on post-processed degree values, the resulting synthetic releases inherit formal differential privacy guarantees without exposing sensitive underlying edge connections to the model itself. Graph analysis extracts essential topological metrics from real-world systems, including social circles, communication records, academic collaboration networks, and web link infrastructures. Within these networks, structural metrics such as sorted degree distributions characterize overall connectivity patterns, while subgraph counts like triangles establish clustering coefficients that reflect community cohesion. Releasing empirical graph statistics directly introduces substantial re-identification vulnerabilities, as specific edge configurations frequently encode private, confidential relationships between identifiable entities. In differential privacy frameworks, neighbouring datasets define the scope of protection. Node differential privacy protects a node alongside all of its incident edges, requiring substantial injected noise that severely degrades utility. Consequently, LEGEND adopts edge differential privacy within the central curator model, where a trusted authority possesses the complete graph. In this configuration, two graphs are neighbours if they differ by exactly one edge. Adding or removing a single edge alters the degrees of exactly two terminal nodes by one, establishing that the sorted degree sequence has a global L1 sensitivity of two. Prior techniques for private graph release typically followed two paradigms: calculating query-specific noise mechanisms for isolated statistical questions or fitting parametric stochastic models to perturb statistical summaries. Query-specific techniques require partitioning a finite privacy budget across every intended question, quickly exhausting utility as analytical queries multiply. Synthetic graph publication resolves this budget depletion by generating an artificial network that permits unlimited downstream queries under a single privacy allocation. Existing generators—including DP-dK parameter perturbations, TmF adjacency filtering, PrivSKG, PrivHRG, PrivGraph, and degree-guided generators like DGG—fit predefined generative algorithms to noisy statistics. However, their structural fidelity remains bounded by whatever underlying structural distributions those fixed stochastic models are capable of expressing. Meanwhile, large language models have exhibited structural reasoning capabilities over text-encoded graphs, but prior language-model generators provided no mathematical privacy guarantees. LEGEND bridges this gap by demonstrating that a language model can act as an expressive structural generator driven entirely by sanitized graph degree sequences. The software architecture of LEGEND is implemented in Python across three modular stages connected by plain text files: reference subgraph extraction, synthetic graph generation, and comparative evaluation. LLMs.title: Exploring the Use of Large Language Models in Critical Discourse Analysis: A Consensus-Based Pilot Study - ACL Anthology
LLMs.titleZh: Exploring the Use of Large Language Models in Critical Discourse Analysis: A Consensus-Based Pilot Study - ACL Anthology
LLMs.content: ##### Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences and humanities (SSH) to support the analysis of complex textual data, raising methodological questions about evaluation and interpretive reliability. This paper explores the use of LLMs in Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA), considered here as a paradigmatic case of interpretive research in SSH, through a preliminary consensus-based evaluation framework. The study reports on a pilot experiment conducted on a small, theory-driven corpus of opinion articles addressing the October 7, 2023 attack and its aftermath. An LLM is asked to answer analytically motivated questions targeting different levels of discourse structure. Its responses are compared with annotations produced by multiple human analysts and aggregated through a consensus-based procedure. The results reveal an asymmetry in model performance: while LLMs align well with human consensus on macro- and superstructural features, they struggle with microstructural phenomena involving implicit meaning. These findings support the view of LLMs as epistemic support tools rather than replacements for human interpretation. LLMs.content: ## Abstract Patients receiving radiotherapy for esophageal cancer may consult large language model chatbots about treatment-related adverse effects, but the safety of their advice is uncertain. We submitted 42 researcher-developed, patient-oriented questions once each to ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Doubao through public web interfaces, obtaining 168 responses. Five blinded expert raters assessed potential harm, accuracy, and perceived empathic communication; information quality, visible source transparency, and formula-based readability were also evaluated. Twenty-one responses (12.5%) were classified as potentially unsafe; six could delay clinical assessment and ten involved potentially harmful self-management advice. Unsafe-response proportions ranged from 7.1% to 16.7% across models, with no statistically significant overall difference (Cochran’s Q = 1.981, *P* = 0.576). Median accuracy and expert-rated perceived empathic communication scores were 4 and 3 (on five-point scales) for every model. Between-model differences were statistically significant but small (accuracy: *P* = 0.001, Kendall’s W = 0.126; perceived empathic communication: *P* < 0.001, W = 0.149). Visible source-transparency indicators were limited, and formula-estimated readability differed across models. These single-query findings indicate that favorable accuracy ratings do not preclude potentially unsafe advice and cannot establish stable model rankings, patient comprehension, or clinical outcomes. ## Funding This project is supported by the following funds: National Famous Old Chinese Medicine Experts Inheritance Studio Construction Project (State TCM Human Education Letter \[2022] No. 75) \[CZ0274-02]; National Famous Chinese Medicine Inheritance Studio Construction Project (State TCM Office Human Education Letter \[2022] No. 245) \[CZ0250-01]; National “100,000 Talents” Support Program for Traditional Chinese Medicine—Qihuang Scholars (Document No. 284 \[2018] of the Ministry of Education); Henan Province High-Level Specialty Development Project in Traditional Chinese Medicine (Oncology) (cz0317-10). ## Ethics declarations ### Competing interests The authors declare no competing interests. ### Ethical standards The study assessed chatbot-generated responses to researcher-developed questions and did not involve patients or patient-level data. AI Product.content: A Korean AI startup might impress an enterprise buyer with a flawless demonstration, only to face a question the presentation never anticipated: *Could your assistant reveal a confidential file to someone who isn’t allowed to open it?* Now, this concern goes deeper than simply document access. That is because customer information may pass through external AI models, while connected tools can modify business records. *A product can perform exactly as promised and still cross a security boundary the buyer cannot afford to ignore.* ## Enterprise AI Security Reviews Reach Beyond Conventional Software Protection Enterprise customers who are evaluating artificial intelligence products are facing security questions that conventional software assessments do not fully address. An AI application may *retrieve corporate records, process them through external models, retain conversation histories, and interact with business software* through application programming interfaces (APIs). And each of these connections introduces questions about **information access, permitted processing, and the consequences of automated operations.** > “Enterprise customers are asking AI startups many of the traditional SaaS security questions, but they are also examining how data, models, prompts, outputs, and automated actions are governed,” [**Bhavdipkumar Gadhavi**](https://www.linkedin.com/in/bhavdipkumargadhavi/) told KoreaTechDesk as discussion on [enterprise security governance](https://koreatechdesk.com/korean-startups-enterprise-security-governance) continues. Gadhavi, founder and director of [*BlockBreach Pvt. Ltd*.](https://blockbreach.in/) and founder of [*Sphragi*](https://sphragi.com/), has worked across *penetration testing, cybersecurity assessments, and internal security and compliance leadership.* His observations highlight **how enterprise AI security reviews must account for the behavior of integrated systems**, alongside their underlying infrastructure. The challenge also extends to understanding the providers supporting those systems. A June 2026 [IBM Institute for Business Value study](https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-06-17-ibm-study-limited-control-and-rising-dependencies-leave-enterprises-exposed-in-the-age-of-ai), based on 1,000 senior executives across 16 countries, found that **91% of respondents did not fully understand their organization’s dependencies across AI vendors, models, and infrastructure**. AI Product.content: Karnataka wants to put 63,200 people through AI training, and it has lined up five technology companies to help. [Telegraph India reported](https://www.telegraphindia.com/edugraph/news/karnataka-signs-mous-with-google-and-four-other-tech-firms-to-skill-63200-students-in-ai/cid/2190093) that the state signed memoranda of understanding with Google and four other tech firms to skill 63,200 students in AI, with the signing taking place at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026. The Karnataka AI skilling programme is a big number on paper, and the details behind it are still thin. The target group is engineering students, diploma students and working professionals. The partners are Google, Salesforce, Pega Systems, Sarvam AI and Gnani.ai. Education Times has also covered the announcement, and the same core facts appear across the Indian business and education press. This is a story about intent, so the framing matters. The reports describe proposed specialised training programmes, not finished ones. Nobody has been trained yet, and the sources don’t publish schedules, fees or enrolment rules. The announcement also lands as capital pours into the sector, a trend we tracked when [India’s AI funding hit $1.6B, up 96% to a seven-year high](https://shattered.io/india-ai-funding-1-6-billion-96-percent-highest-since-2019-tracxn/). Money for startups is one thing. A pipeline of people who can build and run AI systems is the harder problem, and this programme aims at it. The mechanism is the MoU. A memorandum of understanding is a statement of shared intent, not a delivery contract. It usually names the partners, sketches the areas of cooperation and leaves the hard details for later documents. That fits what the reports show here. They name the companies and the subject areas, and they stay silent on timelines. Five companies signed on. Google and Salesforce are the global names. Pega Systems brings enterprise software. Sarvam AI and Gnani.ai are Indian AI companies, and their presence gives the programme a local flavour that a purely multinational line-up would lack. The headline number, 63,200, is a target. The reports do not say how many learners will start, how many will finish or over what period the state expects to reach the figure. A reader should treat it as the ambition the government chose to publish on summit day, and judge the programme later by what it delivers against that number. According to the company, Raon-1 mini is an artificial intelligence (AI) model developed entirely in-house, from model architecture design to training. It adopts a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture that activates only 4 billion of its 30 billion parameters for computation. Combined with Krafton’s proprietary linear attention technology, the architecture improves response speed and reduces inference costs. Krafton said the full version offers improved reasoning and complex task execution capabilities compared with the preview version. It scored 64.9 on MultiChallenge, a benchmark measuring a model’s ability to follow user instructions and constraints across multiple conversational turns, up 5.9 points from the preview version. According to Krafton, the model outperformed all six comparable overseas models. The model also scored 72.3 and 55.9 on GDPval and BrowseComp Plus, respectively, which evaluate AI agents’ task execution capabilities. It achieved the highest scores among comparable MoE models in both benchmarks. Krafton also added adjustable reasoning capabilities. Users can select from six reasoning levels depending on task complexity. The model answers simple questions without a reasoning process while allocating more computational resources to complex tasks. Krafton released Raon-1 mini on AI model-sharing platform Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Anyone can download the model for free and use it for research and commercial service development. Since launching its AI model brand Raon in April, Krafton has released open-source AI models for speech and vision applications. Infra & Chips.content: # Asia made a big AI bet on Nvidia. What happens now? Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world. Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology. Tech-heavy stock indexes in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan went on a rollercoaster ride this week. Markets soared after a [near-trillion dollar surge](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cq62pn6j42jko) in Nvidia's share price but then slumped as concerns about political and regulatory scrutiny hit investor confidence. The chipmaker is a "symbolic bellwether" of the AI trade that is fast becoming key to places like South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia," says Dylan Loh, an international studies lecturer at Nanyang Technological University. From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes. ## Nvidia is everywhere In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist. That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one. For one, Nvidia was able to grow rapidly by outsourcing chip production instead of having to spend heavily to build its own manufacturing plants. It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC. That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ. "The surge in \[Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports". Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island. To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors. On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain. ![Getty Images The DayOne Data Centers Ltd. campus in the Kempas Tech Park, Johor, Malaysia, on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/fc11/live/ba2cd510-e9ec-11f1-b6b1-7951f81135eb.jpg.webp)Getty Images It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics. "Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says. In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to [market research group CBRE](https://www.cbre.com.sg/insights/reports/2026-asia-pacific-data-centre-trends-and-outlook?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=22740080622&gbraid=0AAAAABJKBd4o1u9qgGTURQlobueIy0JvC&gclid=CjwKCAiAq5rYBhB-EiwAhj1RdsP-Hvp1a8i0bN8fYYwmhJMJHQippbNYdi8TH5VKrMrNkxTr_psADhoCmYEQAvD_BwE). The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025. In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". Infra & Chips.content: [disclaimer](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/privacy-terms/disclaimer/). # NVIDIA's Data Center Sales Jump 110%: Can NVDA Keep the Pace Ahead? **NVIDIA Corporation**’s [NVDA](https://www.zacks.com/stock/quote/NVDA) Data Center business remains its biggest growth engine. In the recently reported results for third-quarter fiscal 2027, the Data Center end market’s revenues climbed 110% year over year to a record $107.6 billion. The segment also grew 21% sequentially, accounting for 93% of the company’s $115.8 billion total revenues. Increased spending by cloud providers, AI developers and enterprises seeking more computing power mainly drove Data Center’s revenues higher. Both major customer groups contributed. Hyperscale revenues rose 71% year over year to $60.1 billion, while AI Clouds, Industrial and Enterprise revenues surged 195% to $47.5 billion. NVIDIA stated that demand was supported by Blackwell Ultra systems, the early rollout of its Vera Rubin platform and standalone Vera CPUs (central processing units). Rubin generated nearly $20 billion in its first quarter of production shipments, marking the fastest product ramp-up in company history. The outlook remains strong. NVIDIA expects fourth-quarter fiscal 2027 revenues of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, and management forecasted that fiscal 2028 revenues could grow about 75% year over year. This outlook suggests customers are continuing to invest heavily in AI computing capacity. Still, sustaining this pace will require careful execution. NVIDIA's supply commitments climbed to $390 billion, mainly due to multi-year memory procurement. Data center construction, power availability and customer financing may influence deployment schedules. Overall, demand supports further growth, but supply execution and infrastructure readiness will determine how much of that opportunity NVIDIA can capture. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for NVDA’s fiscal 2027 and 2028 revenues indicates year-over-year growth of 95.4% and 72.1%, respectively. ## AMD and AVGO: Rivals Challenging NVDA in AI Data Centers **Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.**[AMD](https://www.zacks.com/stock/quote/AMD) and **Broadcom Inc.**[AVGO](https://www.zacks.com/stock/quote/AVGO) are two of NVIDIA's major competitors in the AI data center space. Advanced Micro Devices is emerging as a strong challenger in AI computing with its Instinct GPUs (graphics processing units) and EPYC server processors. In the third quarter of 2026, AMD's total revenues soared 44.7% year over year to $13.38 billion. Advanced Micro Devices' Data Center revenues surged 97% year over year to a record $8.55 billion, contributing approximately 64% of total revenues. Data Center revenues were driven by expanding deployments of EPYC processors across cloud and enterprise workloads and initial shipments of Instinct MI450 Series graphics processing units (GPUs). AMD is also expanding its Helios rack-scale systems to compete in large AI infrastructure deployments. Broadcom is another important rival that competes with NVIDIA through its custom AI accelerators and networking solutions. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, the company’s revenues surged 85.5% year over year to $29.59 billion. Strong custom AI accelerator and networking demand drove the quarterly results. Broadcom’s third-quarter AI semiconductor revenues jumped 221% year over year to $16.7 billion. Broadcom expects this figure to reach $21.7 billion in the fourth quarter, reflecting strong demand from AI customers. Its custom accelerator capabilities make it an important alternative for companies developing their AI infrastructure. Infra & Chips.content: NVIDIA is navigating an extraordinary period in its corporate history. In November 2026, founder Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive officer, and board director before being reinstated less than two weeks later. Meanwhile, the company’s artificial intelligence technology is becoming increasingly important in cancer research, drug discovery, medical imaging, and precision radiotherapy. The developments highlight two different dimensions of NVIDIA’s influence: its position at the center of the global AI economy and the growing application of accelerated computing to healthcare. On October 21, 2026, NVIDIA announced collaborations involving AI-assisted protein design, scientific agents, autonomous laboratories, and adaptive radiotherapy. Among its partners was Siemens Healthineers, which is exploring how artificial intelligence and advanced simulation could support more personalized cancer treatment. NVIDIA also has a history of cancer philanthropy through its former Compute the Cure initiative, which supported research institutions, nonprofit cancer-care organizations, and employee fundraising. However, these activities represent distinct forms of involvement in oncology. Compute the Cure was a philanthropic program that has since ended. NVIDIA’s current healthcare initiatives primarily involve commercial technology platforms, computational infrastructure, and scientific partnerships. The central question for oncology is whether these technologies can translate computational advances into faster scientific discovery, safer clinical workflows, and measurable improvements in patient outcomes. ## What Happened to NVIDIA and Jensen Huang in November 2026? NVIDIA experienced an unusual leadership transition in November 2026. On November 12, the company announced that founder Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive officer, and a member of the board of directors, effective immediately. Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s executive vice president and chief financial officer, was appointed interim CEO while retaining her financial responsibilities. Harvey C. Jones became chair of the board. The announcement came amid reporting concerning Huang’s personal conduct and questions involving corporate governance and potential foreign-intelligence activity. These matters attracted considerable public attention. However, allegations reported during the controversy should be distinguished from established investigative findings. On November 23, NVIDIA announced that Huang had been reinstated as president, CEO, and a member of the board, effective immediately. According to the company’s announcement, the board had reviewed the circumstances surrounding his departure and held discussions with Huang. NVIDIA stated that its board had received input from senior levels of the United States government and was confident that Huang’s reinstatement posed no national-security risk. The company also indicated that an independent committee’s investigation would continue. The resignation and subsequent reinstatement marked an extraordinary sequence for a technology company whose products underpin major AI infrastructure projects worldwide. ## Why Does NVIDIA’s Leadership Matter Beyond the Technology Industry? [NVIDIA](https://x.com/nvidia) is more than a manufacturer of graphics processing units. Its hardware, networking systems, AI software, and computational platforms support applications across scientific research, manufacturing, telecommunications, robotics, and healthcare. Advanced Micro Devices is a large US$672.5b semiconductor player that designs the CPUs and GPUs sitting at the core of many data centers, PCs, and gaming systems, so folding in AI inference expertise and closer quantum partnerships speaks directly to how its compute roadmap could evolve. This news goes straight at that claim. The Taalas acquisition directly supports the thesis that AMD can become a more complete AI platform rather than just a GPU alternative to Nvidia. Adding specialized inference designs into future Instinct and system roadmaps lines up with the catalyst around securing multi generation Helios commitments, because customers want both training and inference solved in one stack. The expanded PsiQuantum partnership pushes on a different pressure point in the Narrative, namely that tight supply chains and new workloads could cap how much data center demand AMD can actually serve. Hybrid classical-quantum projects for drug discovery and scientific modeling test ROCm, packaging, and system engineering against Nvidia and Intel, so any bottlenecks would show up quickly in those high profile deployments. Infra & Chips.title: Compal Introduced Rack-Scale Liquid Cooling for NVIDIA Rubin AI Servers - Refindustry
Infra & Chips.titleZh: Compal Introduced Rack-Scale Liquid Cooling for NVIDIA Rubin AI Servers - Refindustry
Infra & Chips.content: Compal Electronics introduced a rack-scale liquid cooling solution based on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, designed for high-density AI computing infrastructure. The system combined direct liquid cooling, rack-level power infrastructure, centralized management, and leak protection mechanisms to address the thermal and power requirements of GPU-intensive workloads. The rack was designed to accommodate up to nine OG231-2-L1 direct liquid-cooled servers, supporting a total of 72 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs. Each server featured eight GPUs with NVIDIA NVLink 6 technology. According to NVIDIA specifications, each eight-GPU system could deliver up to 400 petaflops of NVFP4 inference performance and 24 TB/s of aggregate NVLink 6 Switch bandwidth. The rack architecture integrated direct liquid cooling (DLC) with power infrastructure and centralized system management. Leak protection mechanisms were included to support high-density GPU deployments. The solution targeted AI training, inference, and other compute-intensive workloads. Compal also presented its OX130-8N-L1 NVIDIA Vera CPU rack, designed to accommodate up to 32 compute trays containing a total of 256 Vera CPUs. Each tray featured eight Vera CPUs and one NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPU. According to NVIDIA specifications, the rack could support more than 22,500 concurrent CPU execution environments. “As AI advances from model training toward large-scale inference and agentic applications, customers need more than greater computing performance. They need complete, deployment-ready infrastructure solutions,” said Alan Chang, Vice President of the Infrastructure Solutions Business Group at Compal. Compal showcased the solutions at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26), held November 17–19 at McCormick Place in Chicago, Illinois, USA.
